cards.explanation: The answer is that the king is asked to judge God's people. Verse 2 says, “May he judge Your people with righteousness and Your afflicted with justice.” So the justice and righteousness from verse 1 go straight to work, friends. I think that's a prayer for a king who uses what he's been given. A gift sitting in the box does nobody any good.

The two words are save and crush, friends. Verse 4 asks for the king to “…save the children of the needy…” Notice who gets the king's attention here. It's the kids of the needy, not the people with the fanciest hats. The verse goes on to ask for the king to “…crush the oppressor.” The prayer asks for the king to stand up for the afflicted and to deal with the one hurting them.

The answer is False. Verse 5 says, “May they fear him as long as the sun shines, as long as the moon remains, through all generations.” The prayer asks for it to last through all generations, friends, not one. Sun and moon are the timekeepers here, and I'd say they have a long shift.

The word is flourish, bakers. Verse 7 says, “May the righteous flourish in his days…” Right before it, verse 6 asks for the king to be “…like rain that falls on freshly cut grass, like spring showers that water the earth.” The prayer asks for the righteous to flourish in his days, and that fits the picture of rain on the earth.

The answer is to the ends of the earth. Verse 8 says, “May he rule from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth.” That's a big map, friends. I once thought my bakery counter was a lot of room to cover.

The answer is tribute and gifts. Verse 10 says, “May the kings of Tarshish and distant shores bring tribute; may the kings of Sheba and Seba offer gifts.” These are kings from far-off places, and the prayer asks them to come with their hands full, bakers. Tribute and gifts are what it asks for.

The answer is True. Verse 11 says, “May all kings bow down to him and all nations serve him.” The kings from distant shores are just the start, friends. The prayer widens to ALL kings and all nations.

The answer is that he will deliver the needy who cry out. Verse 12 says, “For he will deliver the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no helper.” After all the bowing and gifts, the prayer turns to the needy, friends. I think that's the part worth remembering.

The answer is False. Verse 12 says he will deliver “…the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no helper.” The ones with no helper are exactly the ones he helps, friends. Nobody has to bring a connection.

The answer is that their blood is precious to him. Verse 14 says, “He will redeem them from oppression and violence, for their blood is precious in his sight.” Their lives matter to him, friends. That's the reason the text gives, and it's a good one.
The answer is all day long. Verse 15 says, “May people ever pray for him; may they bless him all day long.” All day long is a lot of blessing, bakers. Even my oven timer takes breaks.

The answer is an abundance of grain. Verse 16 says, “May there be an abundance of grain in the land; may it sway atop the hills.” That's more than a little, friends. The prayer asks for an abundance, and for it to sway atop the hills.
The answer is True. Verse 17 says, “In him may all nations be blessed; may they call him blessed.” All nations, friends, not just one. This prayer has a very wide reach.

The answer is False. Verse 18 says, “Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who alone does marvelous deeds.” The key word is “alone,” friends. The king is prayed for all through this psalm, but the marvelous deeds belong to the LORD alone.

The word is earth, bakers. Verse 19 says, “may all the earth be filled with His glory.” After the prayer asked for a king to rule to the ends of the earth, it ends asking for the earth to be filled with the LORD's glory. Now that's a big finish.
